Lasika Wellness: Which Channel Earns the Next Ninety Lakh?

Ahmedabad, 14 September 2026

Meera Rathi, Vice-President of Growth at Lasika Wellness, closed her laptop at nine in the evening and looked out over the Prahlad Nagar office park. In eleven days she had to send the finance committee a one-page memo: how should Lasika deploy the additional ₹90 lakh the board had approved for the Navratri–Diwali quarter, when an Indian personal-care brand books close to a third of its annual sales? The money could go to one channel, or be split, but the Nykaa and Blinkit account teams needed a firm number by 25 September to lock festive inventory. Whatever Meera recommended would decide which kind of company Lasika was becoming.

Lasika Wellness

Rakesh Malhotra founded Lasika Wellness in Ahmedabad in 2019, betting that Ayurvedic personal care—dominated by Patanjali and Dabur on one side, Mamaearth and Wow Skin Science on the other—had room for a brand built around one hero category: hair and scalp care, using bhringraj, onion and amla actives, later extended into a ubtan face wash and a small body-care range. By FY26 Lasika employed 210 people, had raised a Series B, and had grown revenue to about ₹21 crore for the year. It sold through four channels: quick commerce (Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart), marketplaces (Nykaa, Amazon, Flipkart), its own website, app and WhatsApp storefront, and general trade—chemists and cosmetics stores reached through a Gujarat-and-Maharashtra distributor. Its label carried AYUSH and BIS marks and its claims were vetted against ASCI's code. Where growth should come from next was the open question.

The situation

Quarterly revenue had reached ₹636.10 lakh, an annualised run-rate near ₹25.4 crore, roughly 21 per cent above the FY26 base. Quick commerce had done most of the lifting: Blinkit and Zepto now moved single-SKU hair-oil bottles the way a kirana store moves soap, and Rohan Mascarenhas, running those accounts from Bengaluru, could point to visible weekly listing growth. But Meera's dashboard, built with Lara Menon's attribution model from Toronto, showed the quick-commerce contribution margin thinning each month as platforms raised visibility fees and Lasika funded deeper discounts to defend its search rank. From Berlin, brand lead Maya Lindqvist flagged a different worry: mystery-shopper photos showed the hero hair oil discounted 20–25 per cent on Blinkit in weeks when Lasika's own site ran none. Rakesh needed a number he could defend to the board in rupees, not a promise about brand equity two years out. Each was right about their own piece of the business; none, alone, told Meera which channel fit.

The people

Meera Rathi — VP Growth, Ahmedabad (protagonist). Owns the memo; wants a decision the numbers and the brand can both survive.
Rakesh Malhotra — Founder & CEO, Ahmedabad. Wants a board-ready growth number; wary of a story built only on discounting.
Lara Menon — Lead Data Scientist, Toronto. Built the channel unit-economics model; wants the decision to follow it, inconvenient numbers included.
Rohan Mascarenhas — Head of Marketplace & Quick-Commerce, Bengaluru. Owns the fastest-growing channel; sees Meera's caution as risk-aversion.
Maya Lindqvist — Brand & Design Lead, Berlin. Watches whether each channel trains customers to see Lasika as premium, or as a discount SKU.

But a quick-commerce customer is worth only ₹1,118 in contribution over a year, against ₹2,881 for one won on Lasika's own site or WhatsApp: nearly two-and-a-half times as much, because the owned channel keeps more of every rupee and lets Lasika message her directly for the next purchase. Exhibit 3 makes the trade-off visual: quick commerce and general trade sit low on margin and data, one earning that with speed, the other with reach into towns Lasika cannot yet serve online. Owned D2C sits highest on margin and data, lowest on reach. Marketplace alone sits mid-table on both—why Lara's Exhibit 2 numbers land near the middle for it too.

Three ways to spend the ninety lakh

  1. Option A — Double down on quick commerce. At CAC ₹200, ₹90 lakh buys 45,000 new customers—the most of any option—and keeps Rohan's listing rank intact through the rush. First orders contribute ₹27.95 lakh, short of the spend; the cohort is worth an estimated ₹503.10 lakh over a year if reorder habits hold. The cost: deeper discounting on the highest-visibility channel just as Maya's brand-erosion worry sharpens, and just as rivals bid up the same festive inventory, which tends to push CAC up, not down, as the quarter runs on.
  2. Option B — Concentrate on marketplace (Nykaa-led festive placement). At CAC ₹250, ₹90 lakh buys 36,000 new customers, whose first orders contribute ₹80.64 lakh—nearest of the three to covering the spend this quarter—and whose cohort is worth an estimated ₹483.84 lakh over a year, within 4 per cent of Option A on 20 per cent fewer customers. The channel is beauty-shopper intent, not impulse, so it supports rather than undercuts premium positioning. The cost: dependence on Nykaa's placement and commission terms, and no reach beyond its beauty-first audience.
  3. Option C — Shift the money to owned D2C and retention. At CAC ₹1,000, ₹90 lakh buys only 9,000 new customers, whose first orders contribute just ₹36.02 lakh. But each is worth an estimated ₹2,881 a year—more than double marketplace—and Lasika keeps the WhatsApp opt-in and purchase history for future offers, a first-party asset that matters under the DPDP Act's consent rules. The cost: 9,000 customers will not move the number the board is watching, and Rakesh must defend a quiet quarter against louder rivals.

Questions for discussion

  1. Using Exhibits 1 and 2, what job is each channel doing—reach, margin, relationship, or availability—and is it suited to that job?
  2. Rohan and Maya read the same exhibits and reach opposite conclusions. What is each weighting that the other is not?
  3. Compare Options A and B on the numbers alone: which is the better use of ₹90 lakh, and does Exhibit 3's reach-versus-margin trade-off change that?
  4. If Meera recommends Option C, what must she tell Rakesh to make a quiet festive quarter defensible to the board?

A note for the learner

Product–market–channel fit asks a narrower question than product–market fit: not whether customers want the product, but which available channels the business can use well, given the product's basket size, margin structure and the relationship it needs with the customer. The channel that grows revenue fastest is not automatically the one that fits—Exhibit 2 shows quick commerce winning on speed and losing on customer value, and Exhibit 3 shows why: the channel that owns the relationship and the channel that grows revenue fastest are not the same one for Lasika, and may not become the same one for years.

A well-reasoned answer works from the exhibits, not instinct: Option A's 45,000 customers and Option C's 9,000 are not comparable without weighing volume against value, and Option B sits close to Option A on cohort value (₹483.84 lakh against ₹503.10 lakh, under 4 per cent apart) with a far healthier margin and less brand-dilution risk.

One defensible path: put the ₹90 lakh into Option B, a Nykaa-led festive placement, rather than further quick-commerce discounting. The numbers justify it alone: marketplace's cohort value sits within 4 per cent of quick commerce's on 20 per cent fewer customers, its margin is more than double, and it does not deepen the discounting Maya has flagged as corrosive. This does not resolve the longer argument for owned D2C; it says only that this quarter's incremental rupee earns more from Nykaa's shoppers than from either extreme. Keep funding D2C retention at its current run-rate in parallel—just not with this ninety lakh.

Lasika Wellness, its people and its numbers are fictional, for teaching purposes. Nykaa, Blinkit, Zepto, Swiggy Instamart, Amazon, Flipkart, Mamaearth, Wow Skin Science, Patanjali, Dabur and the regulatory references describe real Indian market context only.

Chakshu Plant Intelligence: Five Doors Into the Indian Factory

Pune, Thursday 8 October 2026

1. The night before

At a quarter past eleven the twelfth floor of the Kharadi office held a guard, an intern waiting for a build, and Chaitanya Bhide, Vice-President of Go-to-Market at Chakshu Plant Intelligence, rewriting slide nine since six.

Slide nine was titled FY28 Route to ₹90 Crore. The board met at ten next morning in Mumbai and wanted one thing: where the remaining go-to-market money went. Chakshu had ₹6.00 crore left in the second half of FY27 and ₹28.00 crore approved for FY28 — ₹34.00 crore in all — against a target of ₹90.00 crore of annual recurring revenue by 31 March 2028. FY26 had closed at ₹39.40 crore, so that meant ₹50.60 crore of net new ARR in twenty-four months against the ₹21.00 crore added in the twelve months of FY26: 2.4 times the FY26 addition, in twice the time, which is about 1.2 times the monthly pace on a base that has to more than double.

Five routes to market were open; she could fund two properly, three thinly, or one very well indeed. She had four versions of slide nine, each with defensible exhibits behind it and each contradicted by an exhibit she would leave out. The question had stopped being which channel grows fastest and become one she could not phrase: which doors this product was built to walk through.

2. Chakshu Plant Intelligence

Yatin Chitale and Bhaskar Chellappa founded Chakshu in Pune in 2019, after years between them commissioning drive panels across Chakan and Pithampur and building current-transformer instrumentation in Coimbatore. Their observation was mundane and correct: a mid-sized Indian factory could state its monthly electricity bill to the rupee and not say which machine had burned it.

The product was a DIN-rail gateway, the CX-40, clamped to individual feeders, plus a cloud service that turned readings into machine-level cost, idle-load alerts and a monthly energy-per-tonne report. Customers typically cut electricity cost by 6 to 11 per cent in year one. By FY26 Chakshu had 340 people and served plants in twenty-one states.

One decision from that period governs everything Chaitanya can now propose. In February 2023, short of volume and cash, Chakshu signed a five-year original-equipment agreement with Prabha Instruments Limited of Nashik, which sells energy meters through roughly 900 electrical dealers. Prabha would embed Chakshu firmware in its meters and resell the cloud service under its own brand, keeping 55 per cent of the subscription. In exchange Chakshu accepted a clause that looked cheap: in eleven named states it would not sell a software-only subscription to a plant that had bought a Prabha meter from a dealer. In 2023 that was a promise about a channel Chakshu did not have; in 2026 those states hold most of the dealers its partner programme depends on.

3. The industry

Industrial electricity in India is expensive, politically priced and rising. High-tension tariffs vary by state and by hour; discoms such as MSEDCL, TANGEDCO and GUVNL publish time-of-day schedules that reward load shifting; and the Bureau of Energy Efficiency's Perform, Achieve and Trade scheme obliges designated consumers in cement, textiles and steel to meet energy-consumption targets, mandating audits that create a documented reason to buy measurement. Open-access and rooftop solar makes it busier: a plant with captive generation has a complicated bill and no instrument to read it.

At the top of the market sit Schneider Electric, Siemens, ABB and Honeywell, whose suites are excellent, sold by their own field organisations, and cost more than a ₹60-crore forging shop will consider. At the bottom sit dashboards bundled free with meters. Chakshu lives in the gap, and so does the question of who carries a product into it: mid-market factories are reached by electrical dealers, panel builders, automation integrators, energy auditors, solar EPC contractors and Tally resellers, each already in the plant manager's office for other reasons. Meanwhile Zoho, Freshworks and Postman have taught every Indian board that software sells itself — useful when the product is software, misleading when it arrives with a sensor.

Byron Cardoza, hired in 2024 and based in Chicago, sells to Gulf industrial groups, where tariffs are lower, sustainability reporting harder, and utilities such as DEWA and ADDC require certification. Chakshu's largest contract is Bahr Al Hadeed Industries LLC, a Dubai rolling-mill group, at ₹34.00 lakh a year.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

The Series B of ₹210 crore, led by a Singapore growth fund in March 2024, rested on three legs: direct sales would take large plants, Prabha would deliver volume and with it a benchmarking dataset no rival could match, and self-serve would convert the long tail. Two have behaved differently.

Chakshu Lite launched in October 2024 as a software-only subscription for plants that already owned smart meters, priced at ₹96,000 a year and bought by card. Charuta Bapat's team built a clean onboarding flow and the sign-ups came: 9,800 trials in FY26. Only 1,372 of those 9,800 trials reached a live data feed — 14.0 per cent — and 192 became paying customers. Reading a feeder needs a clamp on a live conductor, which needs a licensed electrician, a shutdown window and a plant manager's signature. The team had built a product a buyer could evaluate alone and could not install alone.

The Prabha channel worked exactly as designed and produced a customer Chakshu did not want. Of 4,600 Prabha meters shipped with Chakshu firmware in FY26, 1,240 activated a dashboard — 27.0 per cent — and those 1,240 were 74.3 per cent of new logos but 20.3 per cent of new ARR. Chhavi Bhardwaj's cohort study in April 2026 found 38 per cent of the FY24 Prabha cohort still paying two years on, against 94 per cent of the direct cohort. The dataset had been built. It was a dataset of plants that had stopped logging in.

Bela Chaudhary's partner programme, begun in January 2025, grew from nine partners to seventy-four and became the fastest-adding channel in the company. It is also the most exposed to the Prabha clause, since the dealers who sell Prabha meters and the integrators who resell Chakshu are often the same firms. Yashad Automation & Controls of Nagpur, the best partner by revenue, is a Prabha dealer. Nobody can say how many of the seventy-four are in breach, or who would be liable.

5. The people

Chaitanya Bhide — Vice-President, Go-to-Market, Pune
Owns slide nine; argues Chakshu has run five channels at the scale of one. Not saying: she wrote the FY27 plan funding all five.
Yatin Chitale — Co-founder and Chief Executive, Pune
Wants a number the board accepts first time, and is attached to the Prabha relationship he negotiated. Not saying: he has been sounded out about Prabha buying it.
Bhaskar Chellappa — Co-founder and Chief Technology Officer, Coimbatore
Nine firmware engineers, three requests: Gulf certification, a clamp fittable without a shutdown, a partner provisioning interface. One ships by March 2028. Not saying: he thinks only the clamp changes the company.
Charuta Bapat — Head of Product, Hyderabad
Believes this is a packaging debate: one service sold as three products at three prices would fit three channels. Not saying: no evidence the middle package sells; her roadmap has slipped twice.
Bela Chaudhary — Director, Channel and Alliances, New Delhi
Cites a CAC of ₹2.00 lakh against direct's ₹21.00 lakh and asks why the argument is open. Her variable pay tracks partner-sourced new ARR. Not saying: partner pipeline stages are self-certified and she has never asked for stricter.
Yohan Baptista — Head of Customer Success, Singapore
Runs renewals for everything except Prabha. Observes that the channel a customer arrives through and the one that keeps them need not be the same, and that nobody has costed a direct success manager on a partner account. Not saying: his team is 40 per cent short.
Chhavi Bhardwaj — Lead Data Scientist, Toronto
Built the cohort model. Insists any three-year comparison flatters the cheap channels, because only direct revenue compounds. Not saying: her FY24 cohort holds 22 direct accounts, a thin sample carrying weight.
Byron Cardoza — Vice-President, International Sales, Chicago
Wants the Al Masaf Technical Trading agreement signed: forty Gulf sites in a year is unreachable otherwise. Not saying: its exclusivity routes Bahr Al Hadeed's renewal through Al Masaf, cutting the flagship account.

8. The options as Chaitanya sees them

A. Fund direct enterprise properly. Put the ₹34.00 crore into the large-plant motion on the strength of 128 per cent net retention. Requires roughly doubling 38 account executives, and accepts Exhibit 2's negative contribution for two more years.
B. Make partners the company. Spend on enablement, tooling, margin and the provisioning interface: cheapest acquisition, second-best three-year ratio. Requires renegotiating the eleven-state Prabha clause at a stated ₹9.00 crore, and accepts that Chakshu never meets its customers.
C. Embed in solar installs. Best margin in Exhibit 2 at 42.0 per cent, lowest installation burden after Prabha, a rider on someone else's capital cycle. But it is eleven months old, and Exhibit 4's silence about it is loud.
D. Change the hardware, then fix self-serve. Build the self-fit clamp, reprice, open the long tail. A product decision in the costume of a channel decision; returns nothing before FY29.
E. Sign Al Masaf. Exhibit 6's year-one net of ₹388.00 lakh against a direct loss of ₹122.00 lakh, on forty sites Chakshu cannot reach alone. Consumes the same firmware team as B and D, and hands the flagship account to a distributor.

Chaitanya has begun to suspect the list itself. It presents five channels as five exclusive bets when the evidence suggests the units are wrong: Yohan implies acquisition and retention may need different channels for one customer, Charuta that the variable is which of three products is sold, and Exhibit 5 that the binding constraint is an electrician's calendar. None of the five options is written in those terms.

9. The deadline and the constraints

The board meets at ten on Friday 9 October 2026. Chakshu holds ₹126.00 crore of cash and burns ₹4.20 crore a month: thirty months of runway, and one more funding round to justify. The budget is ₹34.00 crore across the eighteen months to March 2028, against a target of ₹50.60 crore of net new ARR.

The Prabha agreement runs to 31 March 2028; leaving early costs ₹9.00 crore and the eleven-state clause binds until then. Al Masaf's term sheet expires on 31 October. Bhaskar's nine engineers can deliver one of three roadmaps, and Yohan's team is understaffed before any new channel is funded. Plant-level consumption data carries obligations under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 that nobody has mapped against the Toronto pipeline or a distributor's access to dashboards. And seventy-four partners, one OEM and one distributor will read the decision as a statement about their future.

10. Questions for discussion

  1. From Exhibits 1 and 2, what job is each channel doing, and which does a job the company needs done?
  2. Exhibit 2 ranks the channels one way and Exhibit 4 the reverse. What does each measure, and what would you need to prefer one?
  3. Exhibit 3's win-rate column invites a comparison its footnote destroys. Rebuild the partner and direct funnels on one definition.
  4. Exhibit 5 proposes that installation burden explains channel performance better than price or sales effort. Test it against the other exhibits.
  5. The February 2023 Prabha clause was a reasonable trade then. What should Chakshu have asked for instead, and what does that say about the commitments now on the table?
  6. It is Monday 12 October. Chaitanya must publish a plan. What does she publish, what does she stop, and what does she say to the director who asks why FY27 funded all five?

Eleven forty-five

Chaitanya closed Exhibit 4 and opened Exhibit 2 again, as she had thirty times that week, waiting for one to feel more true than the other. Bela's question was unanswered; Byron's deadline was twenty-three days out; in Coimbatore a prototype clamp sat on a workbench nobody had authorised. Product–Market–Channel Fit

A product does not simply need a market. It needs a market it can actually reach, and a way of reaching that market that the economics of the business can sustain. This is the story of how one product-management team in Bengaluru discovered, at some cost, that those are two different questions.

A decision at Chetak Analytics

On the second Monday of October 2026, Meera Iyer, vice president of product at Chetak Analytics, sat in a conference room on the fourth floor of an office park in Bellandur with a single slide open on the screen in front of her: a chart of pipeline by source, flat for the third consecutive quarter. Chetak had built Kavach, a reconciliation and audit-trail analytics product that helped the treasury and compliance teams of non-banking financial companies, or NBFCs, match their loan disbursement records against the formats the Reserve Bank of India required for periodic supervisory reporting. It was, by every account that mattered inside the company, a good product: the eleven customers who had adopted it in the eighteen months since general availability renewed at a rate above ninety percent, and each of them had, unprompted, referred at least one peer institution. Chetak had product-market fit. What it did not have, Meera was beginning to suspect, was a way of getting the product in front of the roughly four hundred and fifty NBFCs in the country whose loan books were large enough to need it.

The company had raised a fourteen-crore Series B round in March 2025 on the strength of that early retention data, and the board had asked, reasonably, for a growth plan. Two motions were already partly built. A three-person enterprise sales team, hired that January, was closing deals with an average contract value of eighteen lakh rupees a year, but each deal took seven to nine months and consumed a disproportionate share of the founders' calendars for reference calls and security reviews. A self-serve signup flow, added to the marketing site in June on the theory that compliance officers should be able to try software the way developers try APIs, had produced four hundred and ten free trial signups and precisely one paid conversion. A third option — signing regional chartered-accountancy firms that already advised NBFCs on regulatory filings as reseller partners — was on the table for the December board meeting but untested. Meera had six weeks to recommend which of these motions Chetak should fund for 2027, and the honest answer, she knew, was not obvious from the pipeline chart alone. It required asking a more specific question than "which channel works," and that question is the subject of this page.

The idea, stated precisely

Product-market-channel fit is the condition in which a product can be acquired, evaluated and purchased by its target customer through a distribution and sales motion whose cost and cycle time the business can sustain at the price the customer will pay. It is a narrower and more operational claim than "the product fits the market." A product can solve a real problem for a real customer — genuine product-market fit, the term popularised by the venture investor Marc Andreessen in 2007 to describe being in a good market with a product that can satisfy it — and still fail commercially because no available channel can economically deliver it to that customer. The idea of testing channel as a variable distinct from product and market took shape over the following decade as go-to-market work professionalised: Geoffrey Moore's earlier writing on crossing the chasm had already shown that different buyer segments require different, sequenced channels, and practitioners such as David Skok, writing on SaaS economics through the 2010s, formalised the discipline of testing a channel's unit economics — its cost of acquisition against the revenue and margin it produces — before scaling it. Product-market-channel fit is the name product and go-to-market teams now give to the resulting test: not "can we sell this," but "which of the channels we could use will actually work, and at what cost."

The problem it was invented to solve is a specific and recurring failure: a team validates that customers want the product, then assumes that any reasonable way of reaching those customers will work about equally well, and picks a channel on convenience, on what a competitor does, or on what the founding team is personally good at. The sentence Meera could repeat in the board meeting without sounding glib is this: a product fits some channels and not others, and finding out which is a separate exercise from finding out whether anyone wants the product at all.

"Wanting the product and being able to buy it through us are two different facts. My job this quarter is to find out, for each segment, whether those two facts are both true — and if they aren't, which one I can change." — the sentence Meera rehearsed for the board

How the fit test actually works

Testing channel fit is a sequence of steps, and the steps practitioners most often skip are the first and the last. The first is confirming that positioning is already settled — who the buyer is, what problem they believe they have, and why they would act now — because channel fit is meaningless to test against an undefined buyer. Chetak's positioning work, finished that spring, had already narrowed the buyer to two named roles inside an NBFC: the head of compliance, who owned the pain, and the chief financial officer, who owned the budget and the final signature. Skipping this step is the single most common reason a channel test produces noise: teams route leads to a sales team or a self-serve flow before anyone has agreed on whose problem, specifically, the product solves.

The second step is enumerating the channels genuinely available — not aspirational ones. For Chetak that meant direct enterprise sales, a self-serve signup flow, and channel partnerships with the regional CA firms already trusted by NBFC compliance teams; it explicitly excluded paid performance marketing, because there is no meaningful keyword or feed for "RBI reconciliation software" that a compliance officer searches before being introduced to the category by someone they trust.

The third step, the one teams most often leave implicit, is mapping each candidate channel against the buyer's actual purchase process rather than against the seller's preferred motion. This is where Meera's self-serve experiment had gone wrong before she understood why: she had built a channel that matched how a developer buys a tool, not how a compliance officer at a regulated lender buys software that will touch loan-level customer data. Under the Reserve Bank of India's outsourcing and IT-vendor risk directions, any NBFC with a loan book above roughly fifty crore rupees is expected to run a documented vendor risk assessment before onboarding a new data-processing vendor — a multi-week internal review involving information security, legal and often the CFO's office. No amount of product quality removes that gate; it is a property of the buyer's process, not of the seller's pitch.

The fourth step is running the arithmetic — cost to acquire a customer in that channel, set against the revenue and margin that customer produces, over the time the channel actually takes to close a deal — and only then, the fifth step, deciding which channels clear a bar the business can live with. That arithmetic is worked through in full in the next section, because it is where Chetak's decision actually turned.

The arithmetic Meera ran

Meera's first pass took the three candidate channels and, for each, estimated the fully loaded cost of acquiring one customer, the annual contract value that customer would generate, and the number of months it would take to recover the acquisition cost out of gross margin — a figure practitioners call CAC payback. Chetak's gross margin on Kavach ran at roughly seventy-five percent, so the formula she used was simple: CAC payback in months equals the acquisition cost, divided by monthly revenue times gross margin.

For direct enterprise sales, aimed at the roughly ninety NBFCs with loan books above five hundred crore rupees, the average contract value was eighteen lakh rupees a year and the fully loaded acquisition cost — two account executives' time-share, a sales engineer, and marketing support over an eight-month cycle — came to about six lakh ten thousand rupees per closed deal. Monthly margin-adjusted revenue on an eighteen-lakh deal is eighteen lakh divided by twelve, times 0.75, or one lakh twelve thousand five hundred rupees. Six lakh ten thousand divided by one lakh twelve thousand five hundred gives a payback of about 5.4 months after close — comfortable, on top of the eight-month sales cycle, for a business with the cash Chetak had just raised.

For the channel-partner motion, aimed at roughly three hundred and sixty mid-market NBFCs with loan books between fifty and five hundred crore rupees, the average contract value was smaller — four lakh twenty thousand rupees — but so was the acquisition cost: a twenty percent first-year revenue share to the partner, about eighty-four thousand rupees, plus an estimated sixty thousand rupees of internal partner-enablement cost, for a total of about one lakh forty-four thousand rupees per closed deal, typically inside four months because the partner's existing relationship shortened the trust-building the direct team otherwise had to do from scratch. Monthly margin-adjusted revenue on a four-lakh-twenty-thousand deal is twenty-six thousand two hundred fifty rupees; one lakh forty-four thousand divided by that gives a payback of about 5.5 months — almost identical to direct sales, despite a deal four times smaller, because the acquisition cost fell in roughly the same proportion.

For self-serve, the acquisition cost per signup was genuinely the cheapest of the three, on the order of forty thousand rupees once content and search costs were spread across signups. But the arithmetic never got the chance to run, because the channel was disqualified before payback entered into it: of Chetak's four hundred and fifty qualified accounts, roughly three hundred and sixty sat above the fifty-crore loan-book threshold that triggered mandatory vendor risk review, and none of those could complete a purchase through a self-serve flow no matter how low its cost per lead. The four hundred and ten trial signups Chetak had collected were mostly individuals inside those larger institutions exploring the product on their own initiative, unable to convert until the transaction moved into a process the self-serve flow was never built to carry.

The second pass matters as much as the first, because channel fit is not a fixed property of a product; it is a relationship between a channel's cost structure and whatever the current price happens to be. If a competitor forced Chetak to drop large-account pricing toward nine lakh rupees, the same direct-sales motion that comfortably cleared the payback bar at eighteen lakh would nearly double its payback period and start to strain the cash the business could tie up in unclosed pipeline. Nothing about the product or the buyer's compliance process would have changed; only the price, and that alone would be enough to turn a fitting channel into a misfitting one, which is the clearest illustration that this is a test to be rerun, not a fact to be filed away.

Eight distinctions worth sitting with

Fit is downstream of positioning, not a substitute for it

Testing channels before the buyer and the problem are precisely defined produces data that looks decisive and is not. Chetak's early self-serve numbers were uninterpretable for months in part because the marketing site addressed "finance teams" broadly rather than the specific compliance officer whose approval the product actually needed; fixing the positioning first is what let the later channel test mean anything at all.

It is not "which channel is cheapest"

The instinct to rank channels by cost per lead or cost per signup is natural and, on its own, misleading. A channel can have the lowest acquisition cost in the portfolio and still be worthless if the buyer's process structurally excludes it, as self-serve was for most of Chetak's market. The right ranking criterion is whether the channel can complete a transaction at all, and only then what it costs to do so.

The informative number is a ratio, not a rupee figure

A channel with a large CAC on a large deal and a channel with a small CAC on a small deal can be equally healthy or equally broken; what determines which is the payback ratio, not the absolute figures. Comparing channels on raw acquisition cost alone, without dividing by the revenue and margin each one produces, is a common and avoidable error.

Channel conflict is a real cost even when both channels individually work

Direct sales and channel partners can each clear their own payback test and still damage the business if they compete for the same accounts — a partner who loses a deal to the direct team stops bringing Chetak new leads, and a direct rep who loses commission to a partner-sourced deal stops prioritising it. Fit has to be assessed for the whole portfolio of channels together, including how leads are routed and who is compensated for what, not for each channel in isolation.

Reach is routinely mistaken for fit

A channel that generates a large volume of impressions, signups or leads is often treated as validated simply because the top of the funnel is full. Chetak's four hundred and ten trial signups looked, on a dashboard, like early traction; they were in fact evidence of interest with no viable path to a close, which is a different and less useful fact.

Fit changes as the company and the market age

A channel that is necessary at one stage — high-touch, founder-led selling that builds the trust a young company has not yet earned — can become an unnecessary drag once the company has references, a track record and brand recognition that let a lower-touch channel work where it could not before. The reverse also happens: a channel that worked when a market was young and undifferentiated can stop working once competitors have trained buyers to expect a certain kind of evaluation process.

What fit cannot tell you

Establishing that a channel can profitably acquire a customer says nothing about whether that customer will renew, expand, or ever reach the value the product promised. It also says nothing about whether the underlying market is large enough to matter, or about the long-run margin cost of leaning on a channel — such as a partner network — that takes a permanent cut of revenue. Channel fit answers one question, "can we reach and close this buyer economically," and confidently answering it should not be mistaken for having answered the others.

The questions worth asking before trusting a channel test

Who, precisely, signs the contract, and who else has to approve it before that signature is possible? What internal process — procurement, security review, legal, a committee — gates the purchase, and does the candidate channel have any mechanism for carrying an account through that gate? What does the channel cost fully loaded, including the people-time a spreadsheet often omits? And is the answer likely to hold for the next four quarters, or is it contingent on a regulatory setting, a competitive dynamic or a price point that could move?

How the shape changes across contexts

In consumer products, channel fit is usually a question of paid, owned and earned media weighed against customer lifetime value and the strength of any organic or referral loop, because the purchase decision itself is instantaneous and made by one person; the channel work is almost entirely about distribution and awareness rather than about a multi-person approval process. In business-to-business products like Kavach, channel fit is a question of sales motion — who talks to the buying committee, who carries the account through internal gates — because the decision is made by several people over weeks or months, and the channel's job is as much to manage that process as to generate awareness. In marketplaces, channel fit has to hold on both sides of the transaction at once: a channel that efficiently brings in demand is worthless if the same or a different channel cannot also bring in supply, which is why many early-stage marketplaces run a deliberately mismatched pair of channels — high-touch, manual recruitment for the harder side of the market, typically supply, alongside broad low-touch acquisition, typically paid or organic, for the easier side.

Company age changes the picture as well. An early-stage company typically has the cash and the organisational attention to run only one channel well, and the discipline to prove that one before adding a second is often what separates disciplined go-to-market work from scattered experimentation — the sequencing Geoffrey Moore described as taking one bowling pin down before aiming at the next. A larger company usually runs several channels simultaneously across segments and geographies, re-testing fit for each new segment it enters rather than assuming a channel that worked for one part of the business will automatically work for another, and accepting channel conflict as a cost to be actively managed rather than a surprise to be discovered.

Three mistakes that look like something else

The first mistake shows up as a healthy top-of-funnel number sitting next to an anaemic revenue number: plenty of signups or leads, almost no closed revenue, for months on end. The underlying error is treating a low cost per lead as evidence of fit without checking whether the buyer's own process allows the transaction to complete through that channel at all. The cheapest diagnostic is to ask a handful of the people who did sign up a single question — who else has to approve this — and see whether the answer routinely names a function the channel has no way of engaging.

The second mistake shows up as a signed partnership agreement that produces almost no partner-sourced pipeline for two quarters. The underlying error is treating the signature on the partnership contract as the finish line rather than the starting line, assuming partners will sell the product with the fluency of an in-house team without being enabled, certified or given a reason to prioritise it over whatever else is in their own book. The cheapest diagnostic is counting how many partner staff have actually completed a live product demonstration or certification; if the number is close to zero, the channel is not operational regardless of what the contract says.

The third mistake shows up as a channel's acquisition cost creeping upward quarter after quarter with no obvious change in tactics. The underlying error is treating a channel that fit at one point in time as permanently fit, missing that the easiest segment of the market has been exhausted, or that competitors have entered the same channel and bid up its cost. The cheapest diagnostic is segmenting CAC by account size or cohort rather than looking only at the blended average, since a rising blended number often hides a mix shift toward harder, more expensive accounts rather than a uniform decline in channel performance.

A fourth, related mistake shows up as a sales team that is closing deals — real revenue, real logos — concentrated in a narrower slice of the market than the one the company set out to serve. The underlying error is mistaking "the channel produced revenue" for "the channel produced the revenue we wanted," when in fact the channel simply found whichever accounts were easiest to reach, which are not always the accounts the strategy was built around. The cheapest diagnostic is comparing closed-deal firmographics against the stated ideal customer profile every quarter, rather than assuming growing revenue validates the target market by itself.

What good looks like

Charvi Health Diagnostics, a Hyderabad-based company building AI-assisted radiology triage software for hospital imaging departments, faced a structurally similar problem two years before Chetak did, and handled it in a way worth holding up as a model. Rather than committing to one channel on instinct, the team ran two candidate motions in parallel for a single quarter on a small, matched set of target hospitals: direct sales to hospital chains' clinical and IT leadership, and a partnership with regional distributors of imaging equipment who already had representatives visiting the same radiology departments every month to service scanners. Both motions produced closed deals, which on a simpler analysis might have looked like evidence that either channel would do. The team went a step further and asked what each channel's economics looked like at scale, not just in the pilot: the distributor channel closed faster and cheaper per deal because trust was already established, but distributor contracts routinely gave each hospital exclusivity to one AI vendor, capping how much of the market that channel could ever deliver regardless of how well it performed. Direct sales was slower and more expensive per deal but carried no such ceiling. Charvi's leadership chose a sequence rather than a single winner: lean on the distributor channel for the first nine months to build a base of reference hospitals quickly, while investing in direct-sales capability in parallel, and deliberately stop signing new distributor exclusivity agreements once the direct pipeline had matured enough to carry growth on its own — trading a short-term cost advantage for long-run headroom, and doing so on purpose rather than by default.

What Meera decided

At the December board meeting, Meera recommended that Chetak fund direct enterprise sales as the primary motion for the roughly ninety large NBFCs above the five-hundred-crore threshold, add the channel-partner motion with two regional CA-firm practices for the mid-market tier, and shelve the self-serve flow rather than continue to invest in it. Her reasoning followed the arithmetic directly: both direct sales and the partner channel cleared a payback period under six months at current pricing, which the business could sustain, while self-serve was not merely weaker but structurally unusable for roughly four out of five qualified accounts because of a vendor risk review neither better copywriting nor a faster checkout flow could remove. Continuing to fund self-serve, she argued, would keep generating a trial-signup number that looked like traction on a dashboard without producing revenue the business could plan around — precisely the first mistake described above, and one she had no wish to keep making. She recommended revisiting the self-serve question annually, since a change in the regulatory threshold, a shift toward smaller and less regulated NBFCs in Chetak's pipeline, or a change in Chetak's own pricing could each move the answer.

The natural next stop for a reader who has followed Meera's reasoning is the module on paid, owned and earned channels, which supplies the vocabulary for classifying the specific tactics inside a channel once fit has established that the channel is worth pursuing at all — and, further upstream, a firmer grounding in positioning, since every step of the test above depended on already knowing, precisely, whose problem the product solves and why they would act now.

Two questions worth sitting with.

If the cheapest channel available to you cannot reach the person who actually signs the contract, is it meaningfully a channel at all, or only a number on a dashboard that resembles one?

How would you know, this quarter rather than at the next board meeting, whether the channel that fit your product last year still fits it today?
