Product–Market–Channel Fit

The near-expert treatment: why a channel is not a tactic but a constraint that reaches backwards into pricing, gross margin, product surface and roadmap; where the arithmetic is decisive and where it is actively misleading; and what competent practitioners argue about when no one is watching.

1. Two decisions, six weeks apart

On 14 August 2026, Nandita Rane, chief product officer of Raghav Instruments in Pune, circulated a four-page board pre-read with an unusual opening line: "We have three channels that all work, and we can only afford the consequences of one." Raghav made a retrofit telemetry module for electric three-wheelers and small commercial vehicles — a sealed unit that clamped onto the battery pack, read cell-level voltage and thermal data, and fed a fleet dashboard that predicted pack degradation four to six weeks before a vehicle stranded a driver. The hardware carried a fully loaded cost of ₹5,890 a unit including installation, logistics and warranty reserve. The analytics subscription ran at ₹180 per vehicle per month at an 86 percent gross margin. Forty-one fleets were live. Renewal on the subscription was 94 percent. Nobody at Raghav doubted that the product worked.

The disagreement was about how it should reach the market. The direct team sold to logistics fleets running three hundred vehicles or more, closed in five months, and produced beautiful economics. The business development team had spent seven months in conversations with a large electric three-wheeler manufacturer about factory fitment, which would put sixty thousand units a year on vehicles before they ever met a customer. And the regional sales manager in Indore had built a network of three hundred multi-brand EV workshops willing to stock the module as a retrofit, on a 22 percent dealer margin. Each of the three could be defended in a board meeting. Only one of them, Nandita had come to believe, was compatible with the company Raghav intended to be in 2030. She had until 30 September to say which.

Six weeks earlier and six hundred kilometres away, Zubin Mistry, co-founder and head of product at Rithika Studio in Hyderabad, had been staring at a different version of the same problem. Rithika dubbed video into eleven Indian languages with voice preservation and lip synchronisation, and it had grown from nothing to 9,400 paying users in fourteen months almost entirely through paid acquisition on short-form video platforms — a channel so responsive in the first two quarters that the team had treated its existence as a strategic fact rather than a hypothesis. In July, two numbers arrived in the same weekly review. Blended cost of acquiring a paying creator had risen from ₹1,180 in the first cohort to ₹4,571 across the trailing quarter. And the finance lead had finally allocated inference cost to plan level, revealing that the top decile of Creator-plan users, the decile that paid acquisition disproportionately delivered, consumed ₹1,764 of compute against a ₹1,499 subscription. Rithika's most efficient channel was importing its least profitable customers, and it had been doing so for a year.

These two companies are not in the same business. One sells a physical object through industrial routes; the other sells inference through an app. What they share is the structure of the problem: both had established that customers wanted the product, and both were discovering that the question of which route could deliver it is a separate question with its own arithmetic, its own second-order effects, and its own capacity to quietly rewrite the product.

2. The idea, its history, and who disagrees about what

Definition. Product–market–channel fit is the condition in which a defined buyer, in a defined segment, can be reached, can complete their own purchase process, and can be closed through a given distribution motion at a cost the unit economics of the business can absorb at the price the buyer will pay — and at a volume large enough to matter. Four clauses, four independent failure points. A channel fails if it cannot reach the buyer, if it cannot traverse the buyer's internal process, if the cost of closing exceeds what the margin allows, or if the channel's ceiling is lower than the revenue the plan requires. Confusing these four is the single most common analytical error in the topic, because on a funnel chart they all look identical: a big number at the top and a small one at the bottom.

The intellectual history runs through four distinct traditions that have never quite merged. Geoffrey Moore, writing in 1991, established that a technology market is not one market but a sequence of them and that each segment requires its own whole product and its own route — the reason a channel that worked for early adopters routinely collapses when aimed at the pragmatist majority. Mark Leslie and Charles Holloway, in their 2006 account of the sales learning curve, argued that a channel's productivity is not a fixed parameter but a function of cumulative organisational learning, which implies that early channel economics are systematically pessimistic and that scaling headcount before yield stabilises destroys companies. Peter Thiel, in 2014, made the blunt structural observation that distribution methods have cost floors and that deal sizes between roughly a thousand and ten thousand dollars fall into a dead zone — too large for a purely self-serve purchase, too small to pay for a human being. And Brian Balfour, writing in 2017, gave the field the decomposition most practitioners now use: market–product fit, product–channel fit, channel–model fit and model–market fit, four dependencies that must hold simultaneously and each of which breaks the other three when you change it. Balfour's contribution was the direction of causation. You do not, he argued, build a product and then select a channel; channels are pre-existing, indifferent to you, and shaped by their own incentives, so the product must be built to fit the channel rather than the other way round.

These traditions disagree, and the disagreement is not cosmetic. Table 1 sets out the propositions each school would sign and the propositions each would refuse. A practitioner who cannot say which row they are standing on will, in a real argument, drift between them and appear to have no position at all.

3. Mechanics: the arithmetic, worked

The operational core is a comparison between two quantities that most teams compute separately and never put side by side. The first is the allowable acquisition cost: how much the business can afford to spend winning one customer, given price, gross margin and the payback period the balance sheet can tolerate. The second is the channel's cost to close: what it actually costs, fully loaded, to move one account from first contact to signature through that specific route.

Allowable CAC = (ACV ÷ 12) × gross margin × payback bar in months
Channel cost to close = Σ over stages of (cost per touch at that stage ÷ cumulative conversion to close)
A channel is economically feasible when cost to close ≤ allowable CAC. It is usable only if it also traverses the buyer's process and has capacity above the plan.

Work it through on Raghav's direct fleet motion. A qualified meeting with a fleet operations head cost ₹42,000 once a field engineer's time, travel and a demonstration unit were counted. Thirty percent of those meetings converted to a paid pilot. A pilot — thirty modules, six weeks, an engineer part-allocated — cost Raghav ₹1,45,000 to deliver. Forty-five percent of pilots converted to a contract. The cost to close is therefore ₹42,000 divided by the product of 0.30 and 0.45, which is ₹3,11,111, plus ₹1,45,000 divided by 0.45, which is ₹3,22,222: ₹6,33,333, rounded to ₹6.3 lakh, or ₹6.8 lakh once a share of marketing was allocated. The pilot term is the one teams routinely omit and it is, here, more than half the cost. A model that treats the pilot as a "stage" rather than as a cost centre understates channel cost by 51 percent.

Against that, the allowable side. A typical fleet ran 420 vehicles. First-year revenue was ₹39.9 lakh of hardware at a 38 percent margin, giving ₹15.16 lakh, plus ₹9.07 lakh of subscription at 86 percent, giving ₹7.80 lakh: ₹22.96 lakh of first-year gross profit against ₹6.8 lakh of acquisition cost. A ratio of 0.30. By the standards of any enterprise software business this is excellent, and for eighteen months Raghav's board had treated it as settled.

It was not settled, because of the third test. Capacity. Four field engineers, at nine qualified meetings a month each, produce 432 meetings a year; at a 13.5 percent meeting-to-close rate that is 58 closes. But the number of Indian fleets running three hundred or more electrified three-wheelers in 2026 was approximately ninety-two. The channel does not merely have a ceiling; it has a ceiling the existing team would hit in under two years, after which the motion's marginal cost rises steeply as the team moves down into hundred-vehicle fleets whose contract value cannot carry a ₹6.3 lakh close. An excellent payback ratio on a market of ninety-two accounts is an annuity, not a growth engine, and the distinction is the whole of Nandita's problem.

The cost floor and the dead zone

Because each channel has a minimum viable cost to close — roughly ₹1,500 for a genuinely self-serve purchase, ₹95,000 for an inside-sales motion, ₹1.4 lakh for an enabled partner, ₹6.3 lakh for field — and because allowable CAC scales linearly with contract value, there is a band of deal sizes that no channel serves well. Exhibit 3 plots both.

Second-order effects, which is where the topic actually lives

The first-order calculation above is the part most teams can do. What separates expert practice is the systematic treatment of what the channel choice does next, none of which appears in the payback formula.

Margin stacking is a pricing decision in disguise. Raghav's dealer channel required 22 percent, taking net unit price from ₹9,500 to ₹7,410 against a ₹5,890 cost, which cuts gross profit per unit from ₹3,610 to ₹1,520 — a 58 percent reduction. You may either raise list price, which re-tests the market box, or absorb it, which re-tests the model box and therefore the allowable CAC for every other channel you run. There is no third option, and the teams that believe there is are usually the teams that have not yet allocated channel support cost against the channel's own revenue.

The channel determines what data you own. Under a factory-fit agreement, the manufacturer holds the customer relationship, the consent for telemetry under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, and the support contact. Raghav would ship sixty thousand modules a year and see almost nothing about how they were used. That is not merely a commercial concession; it removes the input to the roadmap, the basis for any future product-qualified-account motion, and the evidence that would let Raghav argue for a price increase in year three. A channel that severs telemetry buys revenue now by mortgaging the company's ability to know anything in eighteen months.

The channel selects your customers, and your customers rewrite your roadmap. Rithika's paid acquisition did not draw a random sample of creators; it drew the ones most responsive to a demonstration of dramatic output, who were also the ones generating four thousand minutes a month. Six months of feature requests from that cohort pulled Rithika's roadmap towards batch processing and long-form throughput — investments that made the unprofitable cohort more productive. Channel-induced segment drift is rarely noticed because each individual prioritisation decision is defensible; it is visible only when someone asks which accounts generated the top ten roadmap themes and discovers they all arrived through one route.

Channels decay, so fit is a rate rather than a state. Every channel has a responsive stratum that is exhausted first. Exhibit 4 shows Rithika's acquisition cost by penetration decile of its addressable creator base.

4. When the idea applies, and when it misleads

Stated as testable claims, the conditions under which product–market–channel fit is the right lens are four, and they can be checked against both protagonists.

Claim one: the buyer's purchase process is stable enough to model. True for Raghav — a fleet operator's capital approval process is knowable and repeatable. Partly true for Rithika's creators, who buy in a single session on a card, and emphatically true for Rithika's broadcaster prospects, who run legal review of voice-likeness rights before any signature. Where the claim fails — in genuinely new categories where the buyer has no process because they have never bought anything in the category — channel testing produces noise, and the correct move is a small number of hand-run transactions to discover the process rather than a channel bake-off to measure it.

Claim two: the price point is stable over the test window. Raghav's is not; the manufacturer's term sheet contained a six percent annual price-down clause, which means a channel that fits in 2027 mechanically stops fitting by 2030 unless unit cost falls faster. Rithika's is not either, because its effective price is gross of inference cost that varies with usage. Where price is unstable, channel fit must be evaluated as a range and not a point, and the honest output of the analysis is a break-even price below which the channel dies.

Claim three: the channel's capacity exceeds the plan. False for Raghav's direct motion, which is the entire finding of section three. True for its dealer network on paper and false in practice, because only ninety of three hundred dealers ever sold more than two units. Capacity is the most frequently assumed and least frequently measured of the four conditions.

Claim four: gross margin is known at the level the channel operates. False for Rithika until July 2026. A company that cannot allocate cost of goods to the plan level, the segment level or the SKU level cannot compute allowable CAC and is therefore not able to evaluate channel fit at all, whatever its dashboards say.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. The first is pre-fit: a company that has not established that anyone wants the product will cheerfully conclude that its channels are broken when the truth is that its product is. The second is where a channel's value is strategic rather than economic — an early lighthouse account won through an expensive route that will never pay back on its own arithmetic but which unlocks a segment's willingness to evaluate. Evaluating that account on payback is a category error, though so is the far more common move of reclassifying every unprofitable deal as strategic. The third is the learning regime: applying a steady-state payback bar to a channel in its first three quarters will kill motions that would have worked, which is precisely the Leslie and Holloway objection and the reason section ten leaves that dispute open.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product. Once a company sells two products, the tempting move is the ride-along: sell product B through the channel that already works for product A. It fails more often than it succeeds, because channel fit is a property of the transaction and the second product usually has a different buyer, a different approval path and a different deal size, none of which the existing channel is compensated for discovering. The tell is a second product whose entire pipeline is attached to first-product renewals, which looks like efficient cross-sell and is in fact an untested channel hiding inside a tested one. The honest treatment is to compute the second product's channel economics standalone, charging it for the share of the account executive's time it actually consumes.

Two-sided. Fit must hold on both sides simultaneously, and the two sides almost never fit the same channel. The harder side — usually supply — takes high-touch manual recruitment; the easier side takes broad, cheap acquisition. The trap is subtler than the asymmetry: a channel that efficiently acquires one side can poison the other. Rukmini Agri Exchange, an Indore-based marketplace matching farmer producer organisations with food processors, discovered this expensively, and the case is worked in section eight.

Regulated. Indian regulation rarely forbids a channel; it forbids a step. Insurance distribution sits under the corporate-agent and broker categories defined by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India, which constrains who may solicit and how commissions may flow, but it does not forbid digital acquisition — it forbids an unlicensed party from performing solicitation. Medical software touching diagnostic claims engages the Central Drugs Standard Control Organisation's device framework. Lending partnerships sit under the Reserve Bank of India's digital lending directions, which require the regulated entity to own the customer disclosure. In every one of these cases the expert move is to ask which specific step is constrained and whether a differently licensed participant can carry that step, rather than to declare the channel unusable. The teams that get this wrong in both directions are common: some abandon viable channels after reading a circular summary, and others build motions that quietly place an unlicensed party in a regulated step and discover the problem during diligence.

Hardware plus software. Three complications compound. Margin stacks through distributors and dealers who each need their cut. The service network becomes a channel in its own right, often the only one with physical access to the installed base, which makes it valuable and also makes it a hostage. And reverse logistics — returns, warranty replacement, the cost of a failed unit in a village three hours from the nearest workshop — is a real per-unit cost that belongs in gross margin and is almost never there in the first model. Raghav's warranty reserve of ₹640 a unit was the difference between a dealer channel that cleared its cost of support and one that did not.

AI-native. Two new effects. First, variable inference cost makes gross margin a function of user behaviour, so the allowable CAC is no longer a constant for a given plan — it is a distribution, and the channel that delivers the right tail of that distribution is economically different from the one that delivers the median, even at identical cost per acquisition. Second, buyers of AI products demand evaluation before purchase in a way buyers of deterministic software do not, which lengthens cycles, converts the pilot into the dominant cost term, and pushes many AI products up out of the channels their contract values would otherwise suggest. The countervailing force is that model marketplaces, agent directories and platform app stores are genuinely new low-floor channels — but ones where the platform owns the customer, the pricing envelope and the right to compete with you.

The organisational seams. Channel fit is orphaned in most organisations. Marketing owns leads, sales owns pipeline, partnerships owns partners, product owns activation, and finance owns margin — and the test requires all five. What mature companies actually do, as opposed to what they say, is defend the incumbent channel. The channel with a quota has a vice president; the channel without one has a slide. When a partner-sourced deal threatens a direct rep's commission, the outcome is determined by the deal-registration rule and the compensation plan, not by the strategy document, and a great many "strategic disagreements" about channel dissolve on inspection into a comp plan nobody wants to reopen mid-year.

6. Ten distinctions that separate an expert from a competent practitioner

One: fit is a property of the transaction, not of the product. The competent practitioner asks whether the product fits a channel; the expert refuses the question until told which segment and which motion, because the same module fits field sales at 420 vehicles and fits nothing at all at 40. The tell-tale sign is the first clarifying question asked in a channel review. The obvious reading — that a product has a channel the way it has a colour — is wrong because the cost floors that determine feasibility are properties of deal size, and deal size varies inside a single market by an order of magnitude.

Two: reach, traversal, economics and capacity fail identically on a funnel chart. A thin funnel is compatible with four distinct diseases with four distinct cures, and choosing the wrong one wastes a quarter. The expert's tell is that they ask to see the stage at which accounts stop, disaggregated by account size, before offering any opinion. The obvious reading is that a weak funnel means weak demand generation, which is the least common of the four causes in institutional markets.

Three: pilot cost is channel cost. In Raghav's case the pilot was 51 percent of the cost to close. In most enterprise AI sales in 2026 it is more. Teams model CAC as sales-and-marketing spend and book pilot delivery to engineering or customer success, which systematically understates channel cost and produces payback figures that look fine while cash does not. The expert's tell is that they ask who pays for pilots and where that cost sits in the P&L. The obvious reading — that pilots are product work — is wrong because a pilot the customer would not have run absent a sales process is an acquisition cost by function regardless of which cost centre it lands in.

Four: the channel's margin demand is a pricing decision. A 22 percent dealer margin, a 15 percent marketplace take rate, or a platform's 30 percent store fee is not a cost of sale; it changes gross margin, which changes allowable CAC for the entire business, including channels that have nothing to do with the partner. The expert's tell is that they recompute the allowable CAC for the direct motion after a partner deal is signed. The obvious reading — that partner margin comes out of the partner's channel only — is wrong whenever list price is common across channels, which it almost always is.

Five: early channel economics are biased downward, and "we'll learn" is unfalsifiable unless someone writes the curve down. Both halves matter. Yield per rep genuinely does rise with cumulative closes, so a first-quarter payback figure is not a verdict. But the claim becomes an excuse the moment it has no shape. The expert's tell is that when they start a channel they commit in advance to the yield trajectory they expect — closes per rep per quarter, one, two, four, six — and treat a miss against that curve, not against a steady-state bar, as the kill signal. The obvious reading, that you should simply be patient, loses companies more money than impatience does.

Six: blended CAC conceals the only number that decides anything. The relevant figure is the marginal cost of the next increment of penetration, not the average across everything bought so far. Exhibit 4 makes the point: the blended figure was still defensible when the marginal figure had been indefensible for six months. The expert's tell is a request for CAC by cohort, decile or segment, and a visible impatience with the blended number. The obvious reading — that a stable blended CAC means a stable channel — is wrong because mix shift hides inside the average.

Seven: the data the channel denies you is a deferred cost. Partner-led, OEM-embedded and marketplace channels routinely sever the vendor from usage telemetry, identity and the support relationship. The bill arrives eighteen months later as a roadmap that cannot be prioritised from evidence, a renewal conversation with no usage data to anchor a price increase, and the impossibility of ever running a product-led sales motion because you cannot see which accounts are qualified. The expert's tell is that they negotiate data rights in the first partner agreement rather than the third. The obvious reading — that data can be added to the contract later — underestimates how completely the leverage shifts once volume runs through the partner.

Eight: channel conflict is usually a compensation problem wearing a strategy costume. Two channels that individually clear their bars can still destroy each other, and the mechanism is almost always the deal-registration rule and the quota. A partner who loses a registered deal to the direct team stops sourcing; a rep whose commission is halved on partner-sourced business stops returning partner calls. The expert's tell is that they ask to see the comp plan and the registration policy before the partnership deck. The obvious reading — that conflict is resolved by segmenting the market between channels — is only half true, because segmentation lines are drawn in documents and violated in quarters that end badly.

Nine: "structurally unusable" is a claim about a step, and it should be interrogated. Teams conclude too quickly that a channel is impossible because a regulator or a procurement process blocks it, when the block is almost always specific to one step that a differently positioned party could carry. It is equally common for teams to assume the block is soft when it is absolute. The expert's tell is that they name the step, name the regulation or policy that constrains it, and then ask who else in the value chain is already permitted to perform it. The obvious reading in both directions — that regulation kills a channel, or that it can be designed around with better copy — skips the only question that matters.

Ten: the channel that fits your gross margin today may not fit tomorrow's. For AI-native products the loaded margin moves with usage mix and model pricing; for hardware it moves with component cost and warranty experience; for any business it moves with competitive price pressure. A channel is not a fact you establish; it is a relationship between two moving numbers. The expert's tell is that they carry a break-even price or a break-even margin for each channel in their head and can say immediately what would have to happen for the channel to stop working. The obvious reading — that fit, once established, is banked — is the single most expensive assumption in the topic.

7. How this differs across product types and company stages

The arithmetic identity does not change anywhere. Allowable CAC is always price times margin times patience; cost to close is always cost per touch over cumulative conversion. What changes across contexts is which of the four conditions binds first, and it is worth being plain that in several places commonly treated as different, nothing meaningful differs.

Stage changes the picture as much as product type. Before fit, the only defensible channel is the one that lets you learn fastest, which usually means founder-led and uneconomic on purpose. In the first few crores of revenue, the binding constraint is attention: a company can run one channel well and usually runs three badly, and the discipline to prove one before adding another is the difference between a go-to-market function and a set of experiments. Between roughly ten and a hundred crore, the constraint shifts to capacity and to the seams — the first channel's ceiling appears, the second channel is added, and channel conflict arrives as a surprise because nobody rewrote the comp plan. At scale, the constraint is defence of the incumbent channel: the motion with the quota has an organisational immune system, and new channels that threaten it fail for political reasons that look, in the post-mortem, exactly like economic ones.

8. Three worked examples

Raghav Instruments: three channels, three verdicts

Three verdicts, none of them simple. The direct motion is the most profitable per unit of effort and has a ceiling of ninety-two accounts. The dealer motion has the reach and loses money, and the reason is visible in one row: subscription attach collapses from 100 percent to 18 percent, because a workshop mechanic fitting a module has neither the incentive nor the relationship to sell a recurring analytics contract to a fleet owner. Nobody at Raghav had modelled attach rate as a channel-dependent variable; everyone had modelled it as a product property. That single misattribution was the difference between a channel that appeared to contribute ₹1.1 crore and one that in fact lost ₹38 lakh.

The OEM motion is the only one with the volume the board's plan requires, and it is the one that takes away the telemetry, the customer relationship and, through the price-down clause, the margin. It is a real trade with no arithmetic resolution, which is why it is in the closing section rather than this one.

Rithika Studio: a channel that worked until the margin was allocated

Rithika's paid acquisition cleared every test a growth team would normally run. At ₹1,229 of monthly gross profit against an early cost of ₹1,180, payback was under one month. The failure was not in the channel calculation but in the margin input. Once inference was allocated, the Creator plan's gross margin was not a number but a distribution: the median user consumed 640 minutes a month at ₹0.42 per minute, or ₹269, for an 82 percent margin; the top decile consumed 4,200 minutes, or ₹1,764, against a ₹1,499 price. And because the paid creative demonstrated dramatic long-form transformation, the channel over-delivered exactly that decile. Rithika's team recomputed allowable CAC separately for three usage bands and found that for the heavy band it was negative at any acquisition cost, which is a sentence that has no meaning in the standard framework and complete meaning in the real one. The corrective was not a channel change but a model change: a metered allowance of 1,500 minutes on the Creator plan with overage at ₹0.55, which restored margin, reduced the appeal of the product to the unprofitable cohort, and cut paid acquisition volume by a third while raising contribution.

Rukmini Agri Exchange: the failure, and what recovery actually looked like

Rukmini Agri Exchange matched farmer producer organisations with food processors. Supply acquisition was the hard side. In 2024 the growth lead, Parth Bhatia, replaced a field-recruitment motion costing ₹31,000 per onboarded FPO with a channel of agri-input dealers, who already had trust, reach and a reason to visit every village. Signed-FPO cost fell to ₹6,400, a fivefold improvement, and 1,100 FPOs were onboarded in nine months. The metric the team tracked — supply-side acquisitions — improved by every measure.

Two mechanisms produced the gap. The first is adverse selection: dealers were paid on sign-ups and routed the FPOs they most wanted off their own credit books, which were the ones least able to fulfil. The second is the two-sided poisoning effect — a 14 percent dispute rate destroyed processor confidence, and processor repeat orders fell from 61 to 29 percent, which meant the supply the channel delivered had also degraded the demand side the company had spent three years building. A channel can be cheap, high-volume and net-destructive at the same time, and none of the three facts contradicts the others.

Recovery took four quarters and was unglamorous. Rukmini re-based dealer compensation on fulfilled tonnage rather than sign-ups, which immediately caused 250 of 340 dealers to go inactive — the correct outcome, and one the board initially read as channel collapse. It added a three-week assisted first-lot programme staffed by four field agronomists, which raised nominal acquisition cost from ₹6,400 to ₹9,100 and raised the sixty-day listing rate from 31 to 69 percent. And it published a dispute-resolution guarantee to processors funded out of a 1.5 percent reserve on gross merchandise value. Cost per fulfilled lot came down to ₹8,900, still above field recruitment's ₹7,600 but with roughly nine times the throughput ceiling, which is the trade that made the channel worth keeping. The lesson Parth drew was narrower than the one usually drawn from such episodes: the channel was never wrong, the incentive contract inside it was, and the failure was visible in month three to anyone who had been measuring fulfilment rather than signature.

9. Failure modes, their early warning signs, and the cost of late detection

Two of these deserve emphasis because they are the ones competent practitioners still miss. The third row — assuming that attach rates, conversion rates or expansion behaviour are properties of the product rather than of the channel — is the quiet killer of partner strategies, and it is invisible until a channel reaches enough volume for the mix effect to show. The sixth row is invisible almost indefinitely, because each individual prioritisation decision that produces segment drift is locally correct; only the pattern is wrong, and patterns have no owner.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

How long to give a channel before killing it. The structural-economics position is that cost floors are physical facts and that a channel whose cost to close exceeds allowable CAC by more than roughly two times in its first two quarters will not close the gap through learning, because learning improves conversion rates by tens of percent and the gap is multiplicative. Its evidence is the observed stability of cost-per-touch across companies and the regularity of the dead zone. The learning position is that this reasoning is circular, because early conversion rates are depressed by the absence of references, collateral, a trained rep and a known category, all of which are exactly what cumulative closes produce; its evidence is the documented shape of sales yield curves in which the fourth quarter's productivity per rep is triple the first's. What would have to be true for the structural position to be wrong is that conversion improvements of three to five times are routinely achievable within one funding cycle; what would have to be true for the learning position to be wrong is that the companies that persisted and succeeded are survivors of a selection effect that hides an equal number that persisted and died. Both claims are researchable and neither has been settled.

Whether the product should be shaped to the channel. The channel-first school holds that since channels pre-exist and are indifferent, the only degree of freedom is the product, and so a product that cannot be explained in a thirty-second demonstration should not be built if the only affordable channel is self-serve. Its evidence is the observation that products which win a channel almost always carry a channel-specific design feature. The opposing view, held more often by people who build in deep or regulated domains, is that this reasoning systematically excludes the most valuable problems: the products with the highest willingness to pay are precisely those that require configuration, integration and proof, and shaping them to fit a cheap channel is a way of choosing an easier problem and calling it strategy. Their evidence is the substantial number of businesses built on expensive channels serving few, high-value accounts. What would refute the channel-first school is a class of products that became large through a channel nobody could have identified in advance; what would refute its opponents is evidence that deep-domain products systematically underperform on capital efficiency even when they succeed.

Whether platform-owned channels are a distribution advantage or a liability. One camp holds that app stores, marketplaces and model directories are the cheapest distribution ever available to a small company and that the take rate is a fair price for the demand. The other holds that any channel where the platform owns pricing, the customer and the right to build your feature is not a channel but a lease, and that the correct use of it is to convert acquired users to a direct relationship as fast as possible. The disagreement is empirically live in 2026 because the AI ecosystem has made it acute, and it turns on an unresolved question: whether the platform's incentive to keep a vibrant ecosystem is stronger than its incentive to capture the profitable niches within it.

Whether one channel at a time is discipline or dogma. The sequencing view holds that a company has one unit of organisational attention and that parallel channels guarantee two mediocre ones. The portfolio view, more common in consumer, holds that because channels decay predictably, a single-channel company is a company with a scheduled death, and that the right posture is always to be running one mature channel and two immature ones. Both positions are held by people with strong track records, and the resolution — if there is one — probably depends on the decay rate of the channels in question, which is far higher in consumer attention markets than in institutional selling.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this topic produces a channel comparison table. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways.

They compute allowable CAC before they look at any channel's cost, and they compute it per segment and per usage band rather than once for the company, because they know the comparison is meaningless if the denominator is an average of things that differ. They treat capacity as a first-class test rather than an afterthought, which means they can tell you, without preparation, how many accounts their best channel can reach and in what year it exhausts them. They negotiate the second-order terms — data rights, price-down clauses, deal registration, attach-rate responsibility — in the first agreement of a new channel, because they have seen how completely leverage shifts once volume flows. And they hold a break-even condition for every channel they run: the price, margin or conversion rate below which the channel stops working, stated as a number, so that when the market moves they know within a week rather than within a board cycle.

The behavioural tell that distinguishes them most reliably is what they do with good news. When a channel outperforms, the competent practitioner scales it. The expert first asks which cohort it delivered, whether that cohort's margin resembles the company average, and whether the outperformance is the responsive stratum being consumed faster than expected — which is the same event as a channel decaying faster than expected, seen from the other end.

12. What each of them decided

On 29 September, Nandita Rane recommended a sequence rather than a choice, and framed it to the board as an explicit trade of margin for time. Raghav would sign the factory-fit agreement, because it is the only motion whose capacity matches the plan, but with three conditions she made non-negotiable in the term sheet: a non-exclusive clause permitting retrofit sales into fleets the manufacturer did not serve; a data-sharing schedule giving Raghav pseudonymised pack telemetry under a joint controller arrangement compliant with the Digital Personal Data Protection Act; and a floor beneath the price-down clause set at Raghav's projected 2029 unit cost plus 30 percent. The direct fleet team would stay at four engineers, working the ninety-two-account list deliberately as a high-margin annuity that funds the fourteen-month design-in rather than as a growth engine it can never be. The dealer retrofit channel would be stopped, with the finding written down explicitly so that it would not be rediscovered in two years: the channel did not fail on reach or on cost per unit, it failed because subscription attach is a channel-dependent variable and no dealer economics could support selling a recurring contract.

Zubin Mistry's decision at Rithika Studio was narrower and arrived faster. He did not change channel. He changed the model so that the channel's output became profitable: metered allowances, overage pricing, and a reallocation of paid spend away from the creative that demonstrated long-form transformation and towards the creative that demonstrated fast, short-form output. He also stopped the enterprise broadcaster motion for two quarters, over the objection of a sales lead with two live opportunities, on the grounds that each deal required bespoke language-pair work that neither the pilot cost model nor the roadmap could absorb — a decision he described in the operating review as "declining revenue we cannot yet deliver a second time," which is the clearest single-sentence statement of channel discipline in either company's file.

"The channel was never the mistake. Paying a partner for signatures when the business is made of fulfilments — that was the mistake, and it was legible in month three." — Parth Bhatia, Rukmini Agri Exchange, on the 2024 supply-channel decision

Discussion questions

  1. Raghav's OEM channel delivers roughly eighteen times the year-one contribution of the direct motion and forfeits all customer telemetry. At what point, if any, does the loss of data become a larger cost than the gain in volume — and what evidence would you need in 2027 to know whether the non-exclusive and data-sharing clauses were sufficient protection?
  2. Rithika's most efficient acquisition channel systematically delivered its least profitable cohort. Was the correct response to change the model, as Zubin did, or to change the channel? What would have to be true about the creator market for the other answer to be right?
  3. Rukmini's redesign raised nominal acquisition cost by 42 percent and deactivated three-quarters of its partners. Under what board conditions is that decision impossible to get approved, and what would you have had to measure from the first month to make it approvable?

13. Going deeper

Channels: paid, owned, earned supplies the taxonomy for the tactics inside a channel once fit has established that the channel is worth entering at all; without it, channel discussions collapse into arguments about spend. Positioning is the upstream dependency: every calculation on this page assumed a named buyer with a known problem, and channel tests run against an undefined buyer produce data that is precise and meaningless. What a GTM strategy is places channel fit inside the larger sequence of segment, message, motion and metric, and prevents the common error of treating channel as the whole of go-to-market. Your first 100 users covers the pre-fit regime where uneconomic, founder-led channels are correct precisely because their purpose is learning rather than payback. Inbound vs outbound is the practical fork inside most B2B channel decisions and carries the cost-floor arithmetic that determines which is affordable at your contract value. Product-led growth is what channel fit looks like when the product itself is the channel, and it makes the traversal condition — can the buyer complete their own purchase — the central design constraint. Sales-led growth is the corresponding discipline when human touch is unavoidable, and it supplies the yield-curve machinery that the learning school in section ten depends on. Product-led sales, and its product-qualified accounts and leads, is the hybrid that resolves much of the dead zone in Exhibit 3 by using free usage as the reach mechanism and a human only for the traversal step — which is also why the telemetry that partner channels sever is worth defending in the first contract.
